lead: Both readings are about being sent and about what depends on it. Paul had to leave the young Church of Thessalonica in a hurry, sent Timothy back to see how it stood, and now hears that the believers have held firm. In John, Jesus speaks his last public words: he has been sent by the Father as light, to save and not to condemn. An apostle lives for those to whom he is sent, because the Son lives wholly for the One who sent him.

set: This letter is very probably the oldest writing in the New Testament, sent from Corinth around AD 50 or 51. Acts tells how Paul’s preaching in Thessalonica stirred up trouble and how the believers sent him away by night (Acts 17:1–10). He had been with them for only a short time. From Athens he sent Timothy back, because he could no longer bear not knowing how they were (3:1–5). Today’s passage is his answer to the news Timothy brought when he rejoined him (compare Acts 18:5).
str: vv. 6–8: Timothy’s report, and Paul’s relief.
vv. 9–10: thanksgiving, and his prayer night and day to see them.
vv. 11–13: a prayer in the form of a blessing: for the journey, for growth in love, for holiness at the Lord’s coming.
kw: The verb Paul almost always keeps for the gospel of Christ. Here he uses it for Timothy’s report about their faith and love. For Paul, a Church that stands firm is itself good news.
Used in v. 8. It is the stance of someone who keeps his ground under pressure. They were suffering for the faith (2:14), and standing was the victory.
The verb in v. 10, “restore whatever is lacking”. The same word describes the fishermen mending their nets (Mark 1:19). A good faith may still have holes that need a patient teacher.
vv: For we now live, if you continue to stand firm in the Lord.

A short and surprising sentence. Paul is suffering “distress and persecution” (v. 7), and yet his life depends on theirs. This is how a pastor, a catechist or a parent feels about those in their care.
Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and restore whatever is lacking in your faith.
Even this praised Church lacks something. Paul’s joy does not make him careless. The letter he is writing is itself part of the mending, since he cannot yet come in person.
And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, just as we abound in love for you.
Love is asked for as a gift from the Lord. It grows. It also reaches outward: “for one another” and then “for all”, including those who were making life hard for them.
ch: The Catechism points to Paul’s prayer for his Churches as a model of intercession in the first Christian communities: he shares his ministry with them and intercedes for them (CCC 2636). Verse 13 looks to the Lord’s coming “with all his saints”, a phrase that echoes Zechariah 14:5; it may mean the angels, the faithful, or both. In the Great Fast, the passage asks whose faith we carry in our prayer night and day.

r.h: The last public words of Jesus
set: In John’s Gospel Jesus has already left the crowds: “he departed and hid from them” (12:36). The evangelist then reflects on those who did not believe (12:37–43). These verses follow with no place or audience named. They gather up the main themes of his public teaching, and many scholars read them as the evangelist’s summary. From chapter 13 Jesus speaks only with his disciples.
str: vv. 44–45: to believe in me and see me is to believe in and see the One who sent me.
v. 46: I have come as light.
vv. 47–48: I came to save, and the word itself will judge.
vv. 49–50: the word comes from the Father, and his commandment is life.
kw: The verb of v. 44, used for solemn proclamation in John (7:28, 37). This is public, urgent speech, a last call.
A favourite phrase of Jesus in John. A later Jewish saying holds that one who is sent stands for the sender. Jesus goes much further: he is one with the Father who sent him (10:30).
John plays on this word. Jesus did not come to condemn (3:17), and yet no one who meets him stays neutral. Refusing the light is its own verdict (3:19).
vv: And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.
This looks ahead to the supper: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (14:9). Everything Jesus says and does shows us who the Father is.
I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.
The purpose is stated plainly. The light does not come to expose people for their shame, but so that they need not stay in the dark.
for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
Then v. 48 adds that the word he has spoken will serve as judge on the last day. Both are true. The offer is salvation, and a person remains able to refuse it.
ch: The Catechism says that the Son did not come to judge but to save, and that by rejecting grace in this life one already judges oneself (CCC 679). It also teaches that Christ’s whole life reveals the Father (CCC 516). Preaching on this passage, St Augustine explains that when Jesus says the word will judge, he means himself, since he is the Word (in substance).

qa: If Jesus did not come to judge, why do we say in the Creed that he will come to judge?

Both belong together. His first coming was for salvation, and that offer is open to all. The judgment on the last day will reveal the response each person has made to that offer. The judge is the same Lord who died for us (CCC 679).
study: Whose faith do I carry in my prayer, as Paul carried the Thessalonians? What am I doing for them?
“Should not remain in the darkness.” Where do I still prefer the dark to the light of Christ in this Great Fast?
